ExxonMobil attributed the rise in refining margins to a **tight market for refined products**:

- **Demand recovered:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, though jet fuel demand remained below historical levels.
- **Refining capacity fell:** Refinery shutdowns and pandemic-driven underinvestment reduced capacity. Industry rationalization took more than 3 million barrels per day of capacity offline.
- **Supply was further constrained:** Supply-chain constraints and low inventories added to the tightness.

Margins rose well above the top of their 2010–2019 historical range. (2022 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54; PDF pp. 49, 55–56.)

The filing attributes the decline to reduced aircraft production in 2020 and 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic sharply reduced commercial air travel, leading airlines to delay or cancel aircraft orders. Manufacturers cut aircraft build rates, while customers reduced their inventories at extraordinary rates, lowering demand for PCC’s products.

The filing also says production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs adversely affected PCC’s aerospace business. (*Berkshire Hathaway 2022 Form 10-K*, pp. K-12 and K-49.)

Apple’s filing identifies these causes of quarterly net-sales differences:

- **Seasonal demand:** Sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Their timing can significantly affect sales. Anticipation of a launch can affect consumer and distributor purchases; distribution channels also tend to reduce older-product inventory before a launch and stock up on the new product afterward.
- **Demand concentration:** Apple generates a significant portion of sales from a single product, so a decline in demand for it could substantially affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected developments:** These include lower-than-anticipated demand, problems with new introductions, IT system failures or network disruptions, and failures by logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners.

*Source: Apple, fiscal 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 4 and 15.*

The Form 10-K distinguishes the exchange gain, the Foundation contribution and the market-risk effects. The gain figures below are **not additive**.

### Financial results

- **Exchange and subsequent Visa activity.** JPMorgan initially recognized a **$7.990 billion gain**, based on the fair value of the Class C shares received. Second-quarter Visa-related activity—including fair-value changes in the Class C shares and derivatives, and dividends—resulted in a **$7.9 billion net gain**. It was reported in other income within Corporate. (pp. 200, 228)
- **Disposition and expense.** The Firm sold Class C shares in the second and third quarters and contributed some to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation. The contribution was a separate **$1.0 billion second-quarter noninterest expense**. The reported gain and contribution together imply approximately **$6.9 billion of pretax benefit** from those two items; that is a calculation, not a separate reported figure. The filing does not separately quantify the sales proceeds or an incremental gain on the sales. (pp. 200, 228)
- **Cash flow.** The cash-flow statement subtracts the **$7.990 billion initial gain** when reconciling net income to operating cash flow. This is a reconciliation adjustment, not an additional loss. (p. 176)
- **Tax rate.** The Visa gain and contribution were among the factors affecting the income-and-expense mix as the Firm’s effective tax rate rose to **22.1% from 19.6%**. The filing does not isolate Visa’s contribution to that change. (p. 62)
- **Remaining Class B-2 exposure.** At year-end, approximately **18.6 million Class B-2 shares** remained at nominal carryover basis. Their conversion and transfer restrictions depended on litigation; the then-current conversion rate was **1.5430 Class A shares per B-2 share**. The exchange also adjusted the notional of derivatives relating to *pre-2024* Visa B-share sales: those derivatives covered **11.6 million B-2 shares** at year-end and retained conversion-rate risk. (p. 200)

### Market-risk measures

The Firm says the Class C shares elevated both **average and maximum** Corporate, Other and total value-at-risk (VaR). These are full-portfolio figures—not the isolated contribution of the Visa shares. VaR uses an approximately 95% confidence level and a one-day holding period. (pp. 143–144)

| VaR, $ millions | 2024 average | 2024 maximum | 2023 average | 2023 maximum |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Corporate | 23 | 102 | 12 | 17 |
| Other | 25 | 101 | 14 | 22 |
| Total Firm | 47 | 91 | 43 | 57 |

Average total VaR rose **$4 million** year over year, partly because of the Visa shares but also because of purchased credit protection, offset in part by fixed-income volatility rolling out of the look-back period.
